What processing is involved in computing `output` *Tongue y-position*?\n\ni. Frames count as visible only if DLC likelihood > 0.9 and y is finite. For each 50 ms bin, the mean y over the visible frames inside that bin is computed; bins containing no visible frame are marked not-visible. The averaging is done without a loop, via cumulative sums of `y` (zeroed on invisible frames) and of the visibility indicator, indexed by `searchsorted` of the camera timestamps at the bin edges.\n\nii.\n```python\nTONGUE_LIKELIHOOD_THRESHOLD = 0.9   # DLC likelihood; distribution is strongly bimodal\n```\n\n```python\nvisible = (lik > TONGUE_LIKELIHOOD_THRESHOLD) & np.isfinite(y)\n\n# cumulative sums let us average the frames inside every bin without a loop\nyv = np.where(visible, y, 0.0)\ncs_y = np.concatenate([[0.0], np.cumsum(yv)])\ncs_n = np.concatenate([[0], np.cumsum(visible.astype(np.int64))])\nidx = np.searchsorted(ts, edges_abs)                  # (ntrials, NBINS+1)\nlo, hi = idx[:, :-1], idx[:, 1:]\nnvis = cs_n[hi] - cs_n[lo]\nsumy = cs_y[hi] - cs_y[lo]\nwith np.errstate(invalid='ignore', divide='ignore'):\n    mean_y = np.where(nvis > 0, sumy / np.maximum(nvis, 1), np.nan)\nreturn mean_y, nvis > 0\n```\n\niii. Key decision 6: \"**Tongue visibility threshold 0.9** on the DLC likelihood: the likelihood distribution is strongly bimodal (99.8% of frames are <0.1 or >0.9), so the exact threshold is irrelevant.\" The averaging choice is justified against the reference in the docstring: \"As in the reference alignment script the marker stream is aligned to the go cue; here all frames falling inside a bin are averaged (the reference used the last frame of each 3.4 ms bin, which for a 3.4 ms bin is the same operation).\" Step 6 lists the cumsum implementation as a deliberate speedup (\"~50x vs per-bin loops\"). The trajectory records that the papers specify no DLC likelihood threshold, so the AI set one from the observed bimodality.\n\n## 8-c. How is `output` *Tongue y-position* thresholded into categories?\n\ni. Per session, the 40th and 60th percentiles of the binned mean y are computed over **all visible bins of that session's extracted trial windows**, and each bin is assigned: 0 if `mean_y < p40`, 1 if `p40 <= mean_y <= p60`, 2 if `mean_y > p60`, and 3 (\"not visible\") if the bin has no visible frame. Resulting full-dataset distribution 0.098 / 0.049 / 0.098 / 0.755 — i.e. exactly 40/20/40 among the visible bins, with 75.5% of all bins not visible.\n\nii.\n```python\ndef discretize_tongue(mean_y, visible):\n    \"\"\"0: < 40th pctile, 1: 40-60th pctile, 2: > 60th pctile, 3: not visible.\n\n    Percentiles are computed per session over all bins in which the tongue is visible.\n    \"\"\"\n    cls = np.full(mean_y.shape, 3, dtype=np.int64)\n    vals = mean_y[visible]\n    if vals.size == 0:\n        return cls\n    p40, p60 = np.percentile(vals, [40, 60])\n    cls[visible & (mean_y < p40)] = 0\n    cls[visible & (mean_y >= p40) & (mean_y <= p60)] = 1\n    cls[visible & (mean_y > p60)] = 2\n    return cls\n```\n\n```python\nOUTPUT_VALUES = [\n    ...\n    ['low (<40th pctile)', 'middle (40-60th pctile)', 'high (>60th pctile)', 'not visible'],\n]\n```\n\niii. Key decision 7: \"**Per-session tongue percentiles** computed over the visible bins of that session's extracted windows, exactly as the spec states ('per-session discretization').\" The 40/60 split and the fourth \"not visible\" class follow the decoder spec directly. Step 10 Check 2 verified the class balance independently: \"tongue class balance | 40/20/40 among visible bins | PASS ([0.40, 0.20, 0.40])\", and the `--show-processing` plot shows the y histogram with the two percentile cuts drawn on it (Step 7: \"the 40th/60th percentile cuts inside the bulk\").\n\n## 8-d. How is `output` *Tongue y-position* aligned with the neural data?\n\ni. The camera timestamps are session-absolute, on the same clock as the spikes, so the per-trial frame ranges are found by `np.searchsorted(ts, edges_abs)` against the very same absolute bin edges used for the firing rates — bin *k* of the tongue output covers exactly the interval of bin *k* of `neural`. No interpolation or offset correction. Where the video is off (inter-trial intervals, and the leading bins of trials whose go cue is less than 2.5 s after trial start) the bins simply contain no frames and become class 3.\n\nii.\n```python\nidx = np.searchsorted(ts, edges_abs)                  # (ntrials, NBINS+1)\nlo, hi = idx[:, :-1], idx[:, 1:]\nnvis = cs_n[hi] - cs_n[lo]\n```\n\n```python\ntongue_y, tongue_visible = tongue_y_per_bin(f, edges_abs)\ntongue_class = discretize_tongue(tongue_y, tongue_visible)\n```\n\niii. Step 10 Check 3: \"(c) temporal alignment | spikes and video aligned to the go cue | spike times minus `go_start_times`; video binned on the same absolute grid | same\". Step 1 notes the reference `align_markers_between_lims(marker_data, go_times, t_min=-3, t_max=1.5)` also aligns markers to the go cue, so the alignment event matches. Step 2's timing table records that video exists only within `[trial start, trial stop]` and that 3.1% of trials have less than 2.5 s between trial start and the go cue, which the AI accepts as genuinely-unobserved bins rather than filtering those trials (Key decision 3). Step 7's plot review confirms the expected structure: \"the tongue class raster shows licking bouts only after the go cue (or before it on early-lick trials).\"\n\n## 9. How are minor mistakes in the data, e.g. missing data, handled?\n\ni. Seven distinct cases, each handled explicitly:\n- **Session never quality-controlled / no good units** -> session dropped (1 of 174 files; matches the paper's 173 sessions).\n- **Go-cue count disagreeing with the trial count** -> session rejected; non-finite go cues -> those trials dropped.\n- **Ephys covering only part of the behavioural session** (8 sessions) -> trials outside every good unit's `obs_intervals` dropped.\n- **Trial listed in `obs_intervals` but with no spikes at all** -> dropped after binning.\n- **Bins with no recorded spikes because the window extends past the trial boundary** -> kept and left at 0 Hz, deliberately not filtered.\n- **No visible tongue in a bin** (75.5% of bins), or no tongue camera at all -> explicit fourth class 3, 'not visible', rather than imputation.\n- **Missing tone onset** -> nominal 1.85 s before the go cue (never triggered); **missing photostim event stream** -> reconstruct from the trials-table strings; **missing/NaN CCF ML coordinate** -> hemisphere defaults to 'right'.\nIndividual sessions are also protected by a try/except in the worker, so one bad file cannot abort the run.\n\nii.\n```python\ngood = (classification == b'good')\ngood &= np.array([a.strip() != '' for a in anno])\nunit_ids = np.where(good)[0]\nif len(unit_ids) == 0:\n    print('%s: no good units, skipping' % sess_id, flush=True)\n    return None\n```\n\n```python\nkeep &= np.isfinite(go_all)\nkeep &= observed_trial_mask(u, unit_ids, trial_start, trial_stop)\n...\nhas_spikes = fr.sum(axis=(0, 2)) > 0\n```\n\n```python\nif key is None:\n    return (np.full((ntrials, NBINS), np.nan), np.zeros((ntrials, NBINS), dtype=bool))\n...\ncls = np.full(mean_y.shape, 3, dtype=np.int64)\n```\n\n```python\nside = 'left' if (not np.isnan(ml[k]) and ml[k] >= ML_MIDLINE) else 'right'\n```\n\n```python\ndef _worker(args):\n    path, make_plots = args\n    try:\n        return process_session(path, make_plots=make_plots)\n    except Exception as exc:                                   # keep going on bad files\n        ...\n        return None\n```\n\niii. Key decision 3 gives the governing principle: where nothing was recorded *for the whole trial* the trial (or session) is excluded, but where only part of the window is unobserved the data is kept, because \"requiring the whole [-2.5, +1.5] s window to be observed would delete 95% of miss trials\" and make the `outcome` output nearly degenerate; \"Worst-case coverage is 66% of the window, mean ~97%\". Where the measurement legitimately has no value (retracted tongue) an explicit category is used rather than imputation. Step 10 Check 5 enumerates the edge cases and Step 12 records that all of them were found by following up validator warnings rather than suppressing them.\n\n## 10-a. What are the most time-consuming steps of the code?\n\ni. The AI instrumented `process_session` with a `timing` dict per phase and reported: loading + binning neural data ~0.35 s/session, inputs + outputs (including the video stream) ~0.1 s/session, whole session 0.5 s typical and up to ~2.1 s for the largest sessions. Serially this would be ~60 s + ~20 s; with the 16-worker pool the full 174-session conversion took **24.2 s** (0.14 s/session wall clock), and writing the 11.89 GB pickle took a further **20.8 s** — so pickling is nearly half the total runtime. Within a session the dominant costs are the single bulk read of `units/spike_times` (up to ~11.5 M doubles) plus the ~400 per-unit `searchsorted` calls, and the read of the ~680k x 3 tongue-tracking array.\n\nii.\n```python\nt0 = time.time()\nspikes = u['spike_times'][:]\ns0, s1 = _spike_slices(u['spike_times_index'][:])\nfr = bin_spikes(spikes, s0, s1, unit_ids, edges_abs)\n...\ntiming['neural'] = time.time() - t0\n...\ntiming['input'] = time.time() - t0\n...\ntiming['output'] = time.time() - t0\n...\n'duration': time.time() - t_start,\n```\n\n```python\nprint('Processed %d sessions in %.1f s (%.2f s/session)'\n      % (len(results), time.time() - t0, (time.time() - t0) / max(len(results), 1)), flush=True)\n...\nprint('Wrote %s (%.2f GB) in %.1f s'\n      % (args.outfile, os.path.getsize(args.outfile) / 1e9, time.time() - t0), flush=True)\n```\n\niii. Step 6/Step 7 document the bottleneck analysis and the four speedups with their measured gains: single bulk read of `spike_times` (~20x vs per-unit HDF5 reads), `searchsorted` binning instead of nested loops (~100x vs the reference `sliding_histogram`), cumsum video binning (~50x vs per-bin loops), and the 16-process pool (~10x wall clock). The estimate was \"< 2 min with 16 workers, plus ~2-4 min to write the ~12 GB pickle\", well inside the instruction's 15-minute budget, so no further optimisation was pursued.\n\n## 10-b. What loops in the code could have been vectorized to improve efficiency?\n\ni. The AI vectorised the two loops that dominated runtime (spike binning via one `searchsorted` per unit over all trials at once; video bin means via cumulative sums). Several Python-level loops remain, none on the critical path but all vectorisable:\n- `observed_trial_mask` loops over **every** good unit (~400/session) and repeats the same `searchsorted` mapping, even though (as the AI itself established) all good units in a session share one `obs_intervals` set — it could read one unit's intervals once, or compute a single `np.isin` on `start_time`.\n- `tone_onset_times` uses an explicit `for i, s in zip(idx, sample_start)` scan with a running maximum; this is a `np.maximum.at`/`searchsorted` one-liner.\n- The photostim loop rebuilds a full `(n_trials, 80)` boolean mask once per stimulation interval (O(n_stim x n_trials x n_bins)); comparing per-trial onsets against the bin grid once would be O(n_trials x n_bins).\n- The per-unit region assignment calls `map_annotation`, which linearly scans ~14 keyword lists (~200 strings) per unit; There is no rebinning of an already-binned stream: spike times are binned once, straight from the raw times, onto this grid. The video (~294 Hz) is averaged directly onto the same 50 ms grid. This deliberately departs from the reference pipeline's 40 ms window / 3.4 ms stride sliding histogram, because the decoder spec requires 50 ms bins.\n\nii.\n```python\nBIN_SIZE = 0.05           # s, bin width == stride (non overlapping), decoder spec\nNBINS = int(round((OFF_END - OFF_START) / BIN_SIZE))     # 80\nBIN_EDGES = OFF_START + BIN_SIZE * np.arange(NBINS + 1)  # (81,) relative to go cue\n```\n\n```python\n'time_bin_size': BIN_SIZE * 1000.0,\n...\n'n_timepoints': NBINS,\n'bin_centers_sec': BIN_CENTERS.tolist(),\n'neural_units': 'firing rate (spikes/s), spike count per 50 ms bin / 0.05 s',\n```\n\niii. Step 1: \"Our task specifies **50 ms non-overlapping bins**, i.e. bw = stride = 50 ms (documented deviation required by the decoder spec).\" Step 4 records it as an accepted discrepancy: \"Binning | 40 ms window, 3.4 ms stride | - | same | Decoder spec requires 50 ms bins -> 50 ms non-overlapping bins (rates in Hz, same formula count/bin width).\" Step 9's consistency table lists it as \"deviation required by the spec\".\n\n## 3-a. What variables in the raw data is `input` *Time from tone onset in seconds* derived from?\n\ni. `acquisition/BehavioralEvents/sample_start_times/timestamps` (the instruction-tone onsets, session-absolute), together with `intervals/trials/start_time` to attribute each tone event to a trial and the trial's go cue to pick the relevant one. The tone used for a trial is the **last** sample-epoch onset within that trial that precedes its go cue. If a trial has no such event, a nominal 1.85 s (0.65 s sample + 1.2 s delay) before the go cue is used as a fallback.\n\nii.\n```python\nDEFAULT_SAMPLE_TO_GO = 1.85         # s, 0.65 s sample + 1.2 s delay (fallback only)\n```\n\n```python\ndef tone_onset_times(trial_start, go, sample_start):\n    \"\"\"Onset of the (last) instruction tone of each trial.\n\n    The sample epoch is replayed when the animal licks early, so there can be\n    several `sample_start_times` events inside one trial.  The tone that the\n    animal finally responded to is the last sample start before the go cue.\n    \"\"\"\n    ntrials = len(go)\n    tone = np.full(ntrials, np.nan)\n    if len(sample_start):\n        idx = np.searchsorted(trial_start, sample_start, side='right') - 1\n        for i, s in zip(idx, sample_start):\n            if 0 <= i < ntrials and s < go[i]:\n                if np.isnan(tone[i]) or s > tone[i]:\n                    tone[i] = s\n    missing = np.isnan(tone)\n    if missing.any():                                   # fallback, should be rare\n        tone[missing] = go[missing] - DEFAULT_SAMPLE_TO_GO\n    return tone\n```\n\n```python\nsample_start = f['acquisition/BehavioralEvents/sample_start_times/timestamps'][:] \\\n    if 'sample_start_times' in f['acquisition/BehavioralEvents'] else np.array([])\ntone = tone_onset_times(trial_start, go_all, sample_start)[trial_idx]\n```\n\niii. Step 2: \"`sample_start_times` has MORE entries than trials because the sample epoch is **replayed after early licks**\" (405 events vs 368 trials in the first session). Step 10 Check 5: \"Early-lick trials replay the sample epoch, giving several `sample_start_times` per trial -> the **last** sample start before the go cue is used as the tone onset; if none exists the nominal 1.85 s is used (this fallback was never triggered).\" Step 2's timing table records \"go cue - sample (tone) onset | 1.85 s = 0.65 s sample + 1.2 s delay\", which is where the fallback constant comes from.\n\n## 3-b. What processing is involved in computing `input` *Time from tone onset in seconds*?\n\ni. A single subtraction: the absolute time of each bin centre minus the trial's absolute tone-onset time, in seconds, cast to `float32`. It is a continuous, time-varying input, one value per bin, monotonically increasing by 0.05 s across the trial. Observed range over the full dataset: [-1.52, 11.89] s.\n\nii.\n```python\ncenters_abs = go[:, None] + BIN_CENTERS[None, :]\n...\ntime_from_tone = (centers_abs - tone[:, None]).astype(np.float32)   # (n_trials, NBINS)\n```\n\n```python\ninputs = [np.stack([time_from_tone[i], photostim[i]]).astype(np.float32)\n          for i in range(len(trial_idx))]\n```\n\niii. The Step 5 mapping table specifies \"`sample_start_times` (last one before the go cue) -> `input[0]` = 'time from tone onset (s)' | bin-center time minus tone onset time, seconds, float32 | new (spec) | continuous, time-varying\". Step 7's plot review confirms the expected shape: \"Input 0 is a straight line through the trial, crossing zero ~1.85 s before the go cue (the tone onset).\" Step 10 Check 2 re-derived it independently from the NWB file (\"bin centre minus the last `sample_start_time` before the go cue\") and it passed `np.allclose`.\n\n## 3-c. How is the `input` *Time from tone onset in seconds* aligned with the neural data?\n\ni. By construction: the input is evaluated at the centres of exactly the same go-cue-anchored 50 ms bins that define the firing-rate grid (`centers_abs` is `edges_abs` shifted by half a bin), so bin *k* of the input refers to the same interval as bin *k* of `neural`. Nothing is resampled or interpolated.\n\nii.\n```python\nedges_abs = go[:, None] + BIN_EDGES[None, :]\ncenters_abs = go[:, None] + BIN_CENTERS[None, :]\n...\ntime_from_tone = (centers_abs - tone[:, None]).astype(np.float32)\n```\n\niii. The `--show-processing` plot of input 0 against time from go cue is cited as visual confirmation of no misalignment.\n\n## 4-a. What variables in the raw data is `input` *Photostimulation* derived from?\n\ni. Primary source: `acquisition/BehavioralEvents/photostim_start_times/timestamps` and `photostim_stop_times/timestamps`, which are session-absolute laser on/off times (one pair per stimulated trial). Fallback, if those events are absent or empty: the trials table strings `photostim_onset` and `photostim_duration` (onset relative to trial start, `'N/A'` when unstimulated), reconstructed as absolute times via `start_time`.\n\nii.\n```python\ndef photostim_intervals(f, trial_start, go):\n    \"\"\"(n_stim, 2) array of absolute [on, off] photostimulation times.\"\"\"\n    be = f['acquisition/BehavioralEvents']\n    if 'photostim_start_times' in be and len(be['photostim_start_times/timestamps']) > 0:\n        on = be['photostim_start_times/timestamps'][:]\n        off = be['photostim_stop_times/timestamps'][:]\n        n = min(len(on), len(off))\n        return np.stack([on[:n], off[:n]], axis=1)\n    # fallback: reconstruct from the trials table (onset is relative to trial start)\n    t = f['intervals/trials']\n    onset = _decode(t['photostim_onset'][:])\n    dur = _decode(t['photostim_duration'][:])\n    iv = []\n    for i in range(len(trial_start)):\n        if onset[i] != 'N/A' and dur[i] != 'N/A':\n            a = trial_start[i] + float(onset[i])\n            iv.append([a, a + float(dur[i])])\n    return np.array(iv).reshape(-1, 2)\n```\n\niii. Step 2 documents both sources: \"`photostim_start_times` (data = laser power in mW, `control` = stim site code 1/2/4/6), `photostim_stop_times`\" and \"`photostim_onset` / `photostim_duration` / `photostim_power` (strings, `'N/A'` when no stim, onset given relative to trial start)\". What processing is involved in computing `input` *Photostimulation*?\n\ni. A binary (0/1, stored `float32`) time-varying input: a bin is set to 1 if any stimulation interval **overlaps** the bin, i.e. `bin_end > stim_on and bin_start < stim_off`. All intervals of the session are applied against the full `(n_trials, 80)` edge array, so a stimulation is marked in whatever trial windows it falls into, not only in \"its own\" trial. Non-stimulated trials stay all-zero. Over the full dataset 20.0% of trials have at least one bin on.\n\nii.\n```python\nstim_iv = photostim_intervals(f, trial_start, go_all)\nphotostim = np.zeros((len(trial_idx), NBINS), dtype=np.float32)\nif len(stim_iv):\n    for a, b in stim_iv:\n        # a bin is 'on' if the stimulation overlaps the bin\n        photostim[(edges_abs[:, 1:] > a) & (edges_abs[:, :-1] < b)] = 1.0\n```\n\niii. What processing is involved in computing `output` *Tongue y-position*?\n\ni. Frames count as visible only if DLC likelihood > 0.9 and y is finite. For each 50 ms bin, the mean y over the visible frames inside that bin is computed; bins containing no visible frame are marked not-visible. The averaging is done without a loop, via cumulative sums of `y` (zeroed on invisible frames) and of the visibility indicator, indexed by `searchsorted` of the camera timestamps at the bin edges.\n\nii.\n```python\nTONGUE_LIKELIHOOD_THRESHOLD = 0.9   # DLC likelihood; distribution is strongly bimodal\n```\n\n```python\nvisible = (lik > TONGUE_LIKELIHOOD_THRESHOLD) & np.isfinite(y)\n\n# cumulative sums let us average the frames inside every bin without a loop\nyv = np.where(visible, y, 0.0)\ncs_y = np.concatenate([[0.0], np.cumsum(yv)])\ncs_n = np.concatenate([[0], np.cumsum(visible.astype(np.int64))])\nidx = np.searchsorted(ts, edges_abs)                  # (ntrials, NBINS+1)\nlo, hi = idx[:, :-1], idx[:, 1:]\nnvis = cs_n[hi] - cs_n[lo]\nsumy = cs_y[hi] - cs_y[lo]\nwith np.errstate(invalid='ignore', divide='ignore'):\n    mean_y = np.where(nvis > 0, sumy / np.maximum(nvis, 1), np.nan)\nreturn mean_y, nvis > 0\n```\n\niii. Key decision 6: \"**Tongue visibility threshold 0.9** on the DLC likelihood: the likelihood distribution is strongly bimodal (99.8% of frames are <0.1 or >0.9), so the exact threshold is irrelevant.\" The averaging choice is justified against the reference in the docstring: \"As in the reference alignment script the marker stream is aligned to the go cue; here all frames falling inside a bin are averaged (the reference used the last frame of each 3.4 ms bin, which for a 3.4 ms bin is the same operation).\" Step 6 lists the cumsum implementation as a deliberate speedup (\"~50x vs per-bin loops\"). The trajectory records that the papers specify no DLC likelihood threshold, so the AI set one from the observed bimodality.\n\n## 8-c. How is `output` *Tongue y-position* thresholded into categories?\n\ni. Per session, the 40th and 60th percentiles of the binned mean y are computed over **all visible bins of that session's extracted trial windows**, and each bin is assigned: 0 if `mean_y < p40`, 1 if `p40 <= mean_y <= p60`, 2 if `mean_y > p60`, and 3 (\"not visible\") if the bin has no visible frame. Resulting full-dataset distribution 0.098 / 0.049 / 0.098 / 0.755 — i.e. exactly 40/20/40 among the visible bins, with 75.5% of all bins not visible.\n\nii.\n```python\ndef discretize_tongue(mean_y, visible):\n    \"\"\"0: < 40th pctile, 1: 40-60th pctile, 2: > 60th pctile, 3: not visible.\n\n    Percentiles are computed per session over all bins in which the tongue is visible.\n    \"\"\"\n    cls = np.full(mean_y.shape, 3, dtype=np.int64)\n    vals = mean_y[visible]\n    if vals.size == 0:\n        return cls\n    p40, p60 = np.percentile(vals, [40, 60])\n    cls[visible & (mean_y < p40)] = 0\n    cls[visible & (mean_y >= p40) & (mean_y <= p60)] = 1\n    cls[visible & (mean_y > p60)] = 2\n    return cls\n```\n\n```python\nOUTPUT_VALUES = [\n    ...\n    ['low (<40th pctile)', 'middle (40-60th pctile)', 'high (>60th pctile)', 'not visible'],\n]\n```\n\niii. Key decision 7: \"**Per-session tongue percentiles** computed over the visible bins of that session's extracted windows, exactly as the spec states ('per-session discretization').\" The 40/60 split and the fourth \"not visible\" class follow the decoder spec directly. Step 10 Check 2 verified the class balance independently: \"tongue class balance | 40/20/40 among visible bins | PASS ([0.40, 0.20, 0.40])\", and the `--show-processing` plot shows the y histogram with the two percentile cuts drawn on it (Step 7: \"the 40th/60th percentile cuts inside the bulk\").\n\n## 8-d. How is `output` *Tongue y-position* aligned with the neural data?\n\ni. The camera timestamps are session-absolute, on the same clock as the spikes, so the per-trial frame ranges are found by `np.searchsorted(ts, edges_abs)` against the very same absolute bin edges used for the firing rates — bin *k* of the tongue output covers exactly the interval of bin *k* of `neural`. No interpolation or offset correction. Where the video is off (inter-trial intervals, and the leading bins of trials whose go cue is less than 2.5 s after trial start) the bins simply contain no frames and become class 3.\n\nii.\n```python\nidx = np.searchsorted(ts, edges_abs)                  # (ntrials, NBINS+1)\nlo, hi = idx[:, :-1], idx[:, 1:]\nnvis = cs_n[hi] - cs_n[lo]\n```\n\n```python\ntongue_y, tongue_visible = tongue_y_per_bin(f, edges_abs)\ntongue_class = discretize_tongue(tongue_y, tongue_visible)\n```\n\niii. Step 10 Check 3: \"(c) temporal alignment | spikes and video aligned to the go cue | spike times minus `go_start_times`; video binned on the same absolute grid | same\". Step 1 notes the reference `align_markers_between_lims(marker_data, go_times, t_min=-3, t_max=1.5)` also aligns markers to the go cue, so the alignment event matches. Step 2's timing table records that video exists only within `[trial start, trial stop]` and that 3.1% of trials have less than 2.5 s between trial start and the go cue, which the AI accepts as genuinely-unobserved bins rather than filtering those trials (Key decision 3). Step 7's plot review confirms the expected structure: \"the tongue class raster shows licking bouts only after the go cue (or before it on early-lick trials).\"\n\n## 9. How are minor mistakes in the data, e.g. missing data, handled?\n\ni. Seven distinct cases, each handled explicitly:\n- **Session never quality-controlled / no good units** -> session dropped (1 of 174 files; matches the paper's 173 sessions).\n- **Go-cue count disagreeing with the trial count** -> session rejected; non-finite go cues -> those trials dropped.\n- **Ephys covering only part of the behavioural session** (8 sessions) -> trials outside every good unit's `obs_intervals` dropped.\n- **Trial listed in `obs_intervals` but with no spikes at all** -> dropped after binning.\n- **Bins with no recorded spikes because the window extends past the trial boundary** -> kept and left at 0 Hz, deliberately not filtered.\n- **No visible tongue in a bin** (75.5% of bins), or no tongue camera at all -> explicit fourth class 3, 'not visible', rather than imputation.\n- **Missing tone onset** -> nominal 1.85 s before the go cue (never triggered); Per unit, the flattened absolute bin-edge array for all trials is passed to a single `np.searchsorted` against that unit's sorted spike times; differencing adjacent running counts gives the count per bin. No smoothing, no normalisation, no baseline subtraction, no firing-rate threshold on units.\n\nii.\n```python\ndef bin_spikes(spike_times, starts, stops, unit_ids, edges_abs):\n    \"\"\"Firing rates in Hz.\n\n    Reference `sliding_histogram(..., rate=True)` computes\n    (number of spikes in the bin) / bin_width; here the bins are the 50 ms\n    non-overlapping bins required by the decoder specification.\n    \"\"\"\n    ntrials = edges_abs.shape[0]\n    flat = edges_abs.ravel()\n    out = np.empty((len(unit_ids), ntrials, NBINS), dtype=np.float32)\n    for i, k in enumerate(unit_ids):\n        sp = spike_times[starts[k]:stops[k]]\n        idx = np.searchsorted(sp, flat).reshape(ntrials, NBINS + 1)\n        out[i] = np.diff(idx, axis=1) / BIN_SIZE\n    return out\n```\n\niii. Key decision 4: \"**Rates in Hz** (spike count / 0.05 s), as in `sliding_histogram(rate=True)`.\" Step 1 identified the reference function `sliding_histogram(spikeTimes, begin, end, bin_width, stride, rate=True)` as computing \"**firing rates (spikes/s)** = count / bin_width\", and Step 10 Check 3 records the comparison: \"(d) binning | `sliding_histogram`, count/bin width -> Hz | identical formula, 50 ms non-overlapping bins (spec) | same up to the bin size\". Step 6 explains the implementation choice: \"Binning with nested Python loops (as in the reference `sliding_histogram`) is O(n_bins x n_trials) per unit -> replaced by one `np.searchsorted` per unit over all bin edges (vectorised over trials).\" Step 10 Check 2 verified the rates by brute force (`np.sum((sp>=e_b)&(sp<e_{b+1}))/0.05`) for 8 random (trial, neuron) pairs in each of 5 sessions, all passing `np.allclose`.\n\n## 2-c. How is the `neural` data filtered based on quality controls?\n\ni. Units are kept iff `units/classification == 'good'` **and** `units/anno_name` is non-empty (a CCF histology label present). No thresholds on any individual QC metric, and explicitly **no** firing-rate threshold. Sessions with zero good units are dropped (1 file). Result: 69,453 of 272,227 clusters (25.5%), mean 401.5 per session, range 90-923.\n\nii.\n```python\nu = f['units']\nclassification = u['classification'][:]\nanno = _decode(u['anno_name'][:])\ngood = (classification == b'good')\n# reference additionally requires a CCF annotation (histology present)\ngood &= np.array([a.strip() != '' for a in anno])\nunit_ids = np.where(good)[0]\nif len(unit_ids) == 0:\n    print('%s: no good units, skipping' % sess_id, flush=True)\n    return None\n```\n\niii. Key decision 1: \"**Neuron curation = `units/classification == 'good'`**: this column is exactly the output of the region-specific QC classifiers described in the white paper and used by the reference code (`qc_mode='classifier'`). No further firing-rate threshold is applied: the method paper's 2-Hz cut was specific to its ridge-regression encoding analysis, would remove 33% of the units, and the decoder benefits from all recorded units.\" The `anno_name` condition mirrors the reference's requirement that units have \"both ephys and histology\" (`helper_get_neuron_id_area` \"drops units with empty CCF label\"); the AI noted in Step 2 that `anno_name` is \"empty string exactly for the `unlabelled` units\", i.e. the two conditions coincide in NWB. Step 4 reconciles the count with the paper: \"69,453 units with `classification=='good'` (25.5% of 272,227 clusters)\" vs \"69,943 good units, 25.9% of KS2 clusters\" — \"Agree within 0.7%; the small difference is the published-vs-archived QC list.\"\n\n## 2-d. How is the per-trial `neural` data aligned to the event described in the `instructions`?\n\ni. Alignment is to go-cue onset. Spike times and event timestamps share one session-absolute clock, so no resampling or offset correction is required: a fixed grid of 81 edges relative to the go cue is added to each trial's go-cue time to give that trial's absolute bin edges, and spikes are binned against those edges directly.\n\nii.\n```python\nOFF_START = -2.5          # s, signed time from go cue to start of the extracted window\nOFF_END = 1.5             # s, signed time from go cue to end of the extracted window\nBIN_SIZE = 0.05\nNBINS = int(round((OFF_END - OFF_START) / BIN_SIZE))     # 80\nBIN_EDGES = OFF_START + BIN_SIZE * np.arange(NBINS + 1)  # (81,) relative to go cue\nBIN_CENTERS = BIN_EDGES[:-1] + BIN_SIZE / 2.0            # (80,)\n```\n\n```python\ngo = go_all[trial_idx]\nedges_abs = go[:, None] + BIN_EDGES[None, :]\ncenters_abs = go[:, None] + BIN_CENTERS[None, :]\n```\n\n```python\n'temporal_alignment_event': 'Go cue onset (auditory go cue, end of the delay epoch)',\n'off_start': OFF_START,\n'off_end': OFF_END,\n```\n\niii. Step 3: \"the reference DataJoint export stores spike times **relative to the go cue**; the reference marker alignment script (`align_markers.py`) also aligns video to the **go cue** over [-3, 1.5] s\", so go-cue alignment matches both the reference and the decoder spec. Step 4 resolves the format difference: \"Spike alignment | spike times already relative to go cue | absolute session times... | Subtract the go cue time per trial; identical result.\" Step 12 verifies alignment empirically: the processing plots overlay the raw raster and the binned rates on the same axis with the go cue at 0, and the per-time-bin choice decoding rises from chance in the sample epoch to AUC 0.87-0.99 in the response epoch, \"strong evidence that the temporal alignment (go cue at bin 50) ... [is] correct.\"\n\n## 2-e. What is the temporal resolution (time bin size) of the converted data? Is any temporal rebinning applied?\n\ni. 50 ms non-overlapping bins, 80 bins per trial spanning -2.5 s to +1.5 s around the go cue, identical for every trial and session. `metadata['time_bin_size'] = 50.0` ms. There is no rebinning of an already-binned stream: spike times are binned once, straight from the raw times, onto this grid. The video (~294 Hz) is averaged directly onto the same 50 ms grid. This deliberately departs from the reference pipeline's 40 ms window / 3.4 ms stride sliding histogram, because the decoder spec requires 50 ms bins.\n\nii.\n```python\nBIN_SIZE = 0.05           # s, bin width == stride (non overlapping), decoder spec\nNBINS = int(round((OFF_END - OFF_START) / BIN_SIZE))     # 80\nBIN_EDGES = OFF_START + BIN_SIZE * np.arange(NBINS + 1)  # (81,) relative to go cue\n```\n\n```python\n'time_bin_size': BIN_SIZE * 1000.0,\n...\n'n_timepoints': NBINS,\n'bin_centers_sec': BIN_CENTERS.tolist(),\n'neural_units': 'firing rate (spikes/s), spike count per 50 ms bin / 0.05 s',\n```\n\niii. Step 1: \"Our task specifies **50 ms non-overlapping bins**, i.e. bw = stride = 50 ms (documented deviation required by the decoder spec).\" Step 4 records it as an accepted discrepancy: \"Binning | 40 ms window, 3.4 ms stride | - | same | Decoder spec requires 50 ms bins -> 50 ms non-overlapping bins (rates in Hz, same formula count/bin width).\" Step 9's consistency table lists it as \"deviation required by the spec\".\n\n## 3-a. What variables in the raw data is `input` *Time from tone onset in seconds* derived from?\n\ni. `acquisition/BehavioralEvents/sample_start_times/timestamps` (the instruction-tone onsets, session-absolute), together with `intervals/trials/start_time` to attribute each tone event to a trial and the trial's go cue to pick the relevant one. The tone used for a trial is the **last** sample-epoch onset within that trial that precedes its go cue. If a trial has no such event, a nominal 1.85 s (0.65 s sample + 1.2 s delay) before the go cue is used as a fallback.\n\nii.\n```python\nDEFAULT_SAMPLE_TO_GO = 1.85         # s, 0.65 s sample + 1.2 s delay (fallback only)\n```\n\n```python\ndef tone_onset_times(trial_start, go, sample_start):\n    \"\"\"Onset of the (last) instruction tone of each trial.\n\n    The sample epoch is replayed when the animal licks early, so there can be\n    several `sample_start_times` events inside one trial.  The tone that the\n    animal finally responded to is the last sample start before the go cue.\n    \"\"\"\n    ntrials = len(go)\n    tone = np.full(ntrials, np.nan)\n    if len(sample_start):\n        idx = np.searchsorted(trial_start, sample_start, side='right') - 1\n        for i, s in zip(idx, sample_start):\n            if 0 <= i < ntrials and s < go[i]:\n                if np.isnan(tone[i]) or s > tone[i]:\n                    tone[i] = s\n    missing = np.isnan(tone)\n    if missing.any():                                   # fallback, should be rare\n        tone[missing] = go[missing] - DEFAULT_SAMPLE_TO_GO\n    return tone\n```\n\n```python\nsample_start = f['acquisition/BehavioralEvents/sample_start_times/timestamps'][:] \\\n    if 'sample_start_times' in f['acquisition/BehavioralEvents'] else np.array([])\ntone = tone_onset_times(trial_start, go_all, sample_start)[trial_idx]\n```\n\niii. Step 2: \"`sample_start_times` has MORE entries than trials because the sample epoch is **replayed after early licks**\" (405 events vs 368 trials in the first session). What processing is involved in computing `input` *Time from tone onset in seconds*?\n\ni. What variables in the raw data is `input` *Photostimulation* derived from?\n\ni. Primary source: `acquisition/BehavioralEvents/photostim_start_times/timestamps` and `photostim_stop_times/timestamps`, which are session-absolute laser on/off times (one pair per stimulated trial). What processing is involved in computing `input` *Photostimulation*?\n\ni. What processing is involved in computing `output` *Tongue y-position*?\n\ni. Frames count as visible only if DLC likelihood > 0.9 and y is finite. For each 50 ms bin, the mean y over the visible frames inside that bin is computed; bins containing no visible frame are marked not-visible. The averaging is done without a loop, via cumulative sums of `y` (zeroed on invisible frames) and of the visibility indicator, indexed by `searchsorted` of the camera timestamps at the bin edges.\n\nii.\n```python\nTONGUE_LIKELIHOOD_THRESHOLD = 0.9   # DLC likelihood; distribution is strongly bimodal\n```\n\n```python\nvisible = (lik > TONGUE_LIKELIHOOD_THRESHOLD) & np.isfinite(y)\n\n# cumulative sums let us average the frames inside every bin without a loop\nyv = np.where(visible, y, 0.0)\ncs_y = np.concatenate([[0.0], np.cumsum(yv)])\ncs_n = np.concatenate([[0], np.cumsum(visible.astype(np.int64))])\nidx = np.searchsorted(ts, edges_abs)                  # (ntrials, NBINS+1)\nlo, hi = idx[:, :-1], idx[:, 1:]\nnvis = cs_n[hi] - cs_n[lo]\nsumy = cs_y[hi] - cs_y[lo]\nwith np.errstate(invalid='ignore', divide='ignore'):\n    mean_y = np.where(nvis > 0, sumy / np.maximum(nvis, 1), np.nan)\nreturn mean_y, nvis > 0\n```\n\niii. Key decision 6: \"**Tongue visibility threshold 0.9** on the DLC likelihood: the likelihood distribution is strongly bimodal (99.8% of frames are <0.1 or >0.9), so the exact threshold is irrelevant.\" The averaging choice is justified against the reference in the docstring: \"As in the reference alignment script the marker stream is aligned to the go cue; here all frames falling inside a bin are averaged (the reference used the last frame of each 3.4 ms bin, which for a 3.4 ms bin is the same operation).\" Step 6 lists the cumsum implementation as a deliberate speedup (\"~50x vs per-bin loops\"). The trajectory records that the papers specify no DLC likelihood threshold, so the AI set one from the observed bimodality.\n\n## 8-c. How is `output` *Tongue y-position* thresholded into categories?\n\ni. Per session, the 40th and 60th percentiles of the binned mean y are computed over **all visible bins of that session's extracted trial windows**, and each bin is assigned: 0 if `mean_y < p40`, 1 if `p40 <= mean_y <= p60`, 2 if `mean_y > p60`, and 3 (\"not visible\") if the bin has no visible frame. Resulting full-dataset distribution 0.098 / 0.049 / 0.098 / 0.755 — i.e. exactly 40/20/40 among the visible bins, with 75.5% of all bins not visible.\n\nii.\n```python\ndef discretize_tongue(mean_y, visible):\n    \"\"\"0: < 40th pctile, 1: 40-60th pctile, 2: > 60th pctile, 3: not visible.\n\n    Percentiles are computed per session over all bins in which the tongue is visible.\n    \"\"\"\n    cls = np.full(mean_y.shape, 3, dtype=np.int64)\n    vals = mean_y[visible]\n    if vals.size == 0:\n        return cls\n    p40, p60 = np.percentile(vals, [40, 60])\n    cls[visible & (mean_y < p40)] = 0\n    cls[visible & (mean_y >= p40) & (mean_y <= p60)] = 1\n    cls[visible & (mean_y > p60)] = 2\n    return cls\n```\n\n```python\nOUTPUT_VALUES = [\n    ...\n    ['low (<40th pctile)', 'middle (40-60th pctile)', 'high (>60th pctile)', 'not visible'],\n]\n```\n\niii. How are minor mistakes in the data, e.g. missing data, handled?\n\ni. Seven distinct cases, each handled explicitly:\n- **Session never quality-controlled / no good units** -> session dropped (1 of 174 files; matches the paper's 173 sessions).\n- **Go-cue count disagreeing with the trial count** -> session rejected; Do NOT look outside this project directory.\n\n**Goal**: Understand how the original authors loaded and processed their data.\n\n**Actions**:\n- Look for documentation or README files in the `/app/code` directory\n# Decisions\n\n## 1-a. How are **all the data** for all subjects, sessions, and trials loaded in?\n\ni. The dataset is distributed as one NWB file per session under `data/sub-<subject_id>/`. All sessions are found with a single glob over that layout, and each file is opened with `pynwb` and processed once. Subjects, trials, and units are then read from within each file (`nwb.subject`, `nwb.trials`, `nwb.units`, `nwb.acquisition`).\n\nii. Finding all data:\n```python\nfiles = sorted(glob.glob(os.path.join(DATA_DIR, 'sub-*', '*.nwb')))\n...\nfor i, path in enumerate(files, 1):\n    res = process_session(path)\n```\n\nLoading one session:\n```python\nwith NWBHDF5IO(path, mode='r', load_namespaces=True) as io:\n    nwb = io.read()\n    units = nwb.units\n    trials = nwb.trials.to_dataframe()\n    bev = nwb.acquisition['BehavioralEvents'].time_series\n```\n\niii. NWB is the published format for this dataset and `pynwb` is its standard reader. Since there is one file per session, the directory listing is the complete set of sessions and a glob is sufficient; sorting it makes the session order deterministic. The resulting counts (174 files, 28 subjects) match `assetsSummary` in `data/dandiset.yaml`.\n\n## 1-b. How are the data split into subjects?\n\ni. Each NWB file records its animal in `nwb.subject.subject_id`, a numeric string such as `'440956'`. That value is read for every session and carried through to assembly, where `subjects` is the sorted set of unique ids and `subject_idx` gives each session's index into that list.\n\nii. Per session:\n```python\nreturn {\n    'session_id': nwb.identifier,\n    'subject': nwb.subject.subject_id,\n    ...\n```\n\nAt assembly:\n```python\nsubjects = sorted({r['subject'] for r in results})\nsub_ix = {s: i for i, s in enumerate(subjects)}\n...\n'subjects': subjects,\n'subject_idx': np.array([sub_ix[r['subject']] for r in results], np.int32),\n```\n\niii. `subject_id` is the canonical animal identifier in the file, and the containing folder name (`sub-440956`) is derived from it, so no separate grouping step is needed. This gives 28 subjects with 3-10 sessions each, matching the dandiset. The numeric id differs from the mouse name used in the papers — `nwb.identifier` is e.g. `SC015_20190207_120657_s1`, so subject `440956` is mouse `SC015` — but the numeric id is what the NWB subject field provides, so it is used directly.\n\n## 1-c. How are the data split into sessions?\n\ni. One NWB file is one session, so no grouping or splitting is needed. Each session is identified by `nwb.identifier` (e.g. `SC015_20190207_120657_s1`, encoding mouse, date, time and session number), recorded per session and also listed in `metadata['session_info']`. Session order in the output follows the sorted file list.\n\nii.\n```python\nfiles = sorted(glob.glob(os.path.join(DATA_DIR, 'sub-*', '*.nwb')))\n```\n\n```python\n'session_id': nwb.identifier,\n```\n\n```python\n'session_info': [\n    {'session_id': r['session_id'], 'subject': r['subject'],\n     'n_trials': r['n_trials'], 'n_units': r['n_units']}\n    for r in results\n],\n```\n\niii. The dandiset already stores one session per file, so the file boundary is the session boundary and nothing has to be inferred. Because the filename embeds the acquisition timestamp (`sub-440956_ses-20190207T120657_...`), sorting the paths puts sessions in chronological order within each subject. 173 of the 174 files reach the output; the one exception is dropped for having no quality-controlled units (see 2-c).\n\n## 1-d. Are the data correctly split into trials?\n\ni. Trials come from the NWB trials table (`nwb.trials`), one row per behavioural trial, with exactly one go-cue event per row. The row count is checked against the number of go-cue events.\n\nii.\n```python\ntrials = nwb.trials.to_dataframe()\ngo = np.asarray(bev['go_start_times'].timestamps)\nassert len(go) == len(trials), f'{len(go)} go cues vs {len(trials)} trials'\n```\n\niii. Trials are clearly defined by the trials table, so it is used directly rather than re-deriving boundaries from the event streams. `go_start_times` has exactly one event per trial in all 174 sessions, which makes the mapping unambiguous. This is not true of the other trial-phase events: `sample_start_times` and `delay_start_times` can have several entries per trial, because a lick during the sample or delay replays that epoch.\n\n## 1-e. How are trials filtered based on quality controls?\n\ni. Trials are filtered only for absence of spike data, in two cases. First, trials outside `units/obs_intervals`: in 8 sessions the ephys recording starts after the behaviour, leaving up to 376 leading trials with no spikes. Second, `free_water` trials, which have no spikes anywhere in the window even though `obs_intervals` covers them. A session is dropped entirely if fewer than 2 trials survive. No behavioural quality filter is applied.\n\nii.\n```python\n# filter behavioral trials with no spike data\noi_off = np.asarray(units['obs_intervals'].data)\noi_start = np.concatenate([[0], oi_off[:-1]])\nobs = np.asarray(units['obs_intervals'].target.data)[oi_start[good[0]]:oi_off[good[0]]]\nkeep = np.isin(np.round(trials['start_time'].values, 4), np.round(obs[:, 0], 4))\nassert keep.sum() == len(obs), f'{keep.sum()} matched vs {len(obs)} observed'\n\n# filter no water trials\nkeep &= trials['free_water'].values == 0\nif keep.sum() < 2:\n    return None\ntrials = trials[keep]\ngo = go[keep]\n```\n\niii. `obs_intervals` is the file's own record of which trials were observed, and its start times match `trials.start_time`, which makes the mapping exact. The `free_water` exclusion was found empirically — those trials are covered by `obs_intervals` yet contain no spikes at all — and accounts for 2,449 of the 2,451 all-zero trials remaining after the `obs_intervals` filter.\n\nEarly-lick and no-response (`ignore`) trials are deliberately kept, even though the data paper states \"Early lick trials and no response trials were excluded for analysis\", because both are required decoder outputs here. The 2-trial minimum is the target format's requirement.\n\nTogether these remove 3,510 of the 94,370 trials in the retained sessions (3.7%), leaving 90,860.\n\n## 2-a. What variables in the raw data is the final `neural` data derived from?\n\ni. Neural data is derived from `units/spike_times`, the sorted spike times of each unit in session-absolute seconds. Only units with `classification == 'good'` contribute (see 2-c). The go-cue times (`BehavioralEvents/go_start_times`) are the other input, used to place the bin edges.\n\nii.\n```python\noffs = np.asarray(units['spike_times'].data)\nallst = np.asarray(units['spike_times'].target.data)\nstarts = np.concatenate([[0], offs[:-1]])\n\nedges = (go[:, None] + REL_EDGES[None, :]).ravel()\nrates = np.empty((good.size, n_trials, N_BINS), np.float32)\nfor r, u in enumerate(good):\n    s = allst[starts[u]:offs[u]]\n```\n\niii. `spike_times` is the only neural representation in the file, so firing rates are computed from it directly.\n\n## 2-b. How is the `neural` data processed?\n\ni. Spike times are converted to per-bin firing rates in Hz. For each good unit, the bin edges for every trial are built as one flat array of absolute times, `np.searchsorted` gives the running spike count at each edge, and differencing adjacent counts gives the spike count per bin. Counts are divided by the bin width to give Hz. No smoothing, normalisation, or baseline subtraction is applied.\n\nii.\n```python\nedges = (go[:, None] + REL_EDGES[None, :]).ravel()\nrates = np.empty((good.size, n_trials, N_BINS), np.float32)\nfor r, u in enumerate(good):\n    s = allst[starts[u]:offs[u]]\n    # running spike total at each edge; differencing gives the count per bin\n    pos = np.searchsorted(s, edges).reshape(n_trials, N_BINS + 1)\n    rates[r] = np.diff(pos, axis=1)\nrates /= BIN                                  # counts -> Hz\n```\n\niii. Firing rate is computed from the binned spike count over the 50 ms window defined in the instructions. This also matches the reference code, which calls `sliding_histogram(..., rate=True)` and returns `binSpikes / bin_width`.\n\n## 2-c. How is the `neural` data filtered based on quality controls?\n\ni. Only units with `units/classification == 'good'` are kept. No thresholds are applied to any individual quality metric. A session with no such units is dropped entirely. This retains 69,453 of 272,227 units (25.5%), a median of 390 per session.\n\nii.\n```python\n# ---- units: QC classifier verdict ----------------------------------\ncls = _text(units['classification'])\ngood = np.flatnonzero(cls == 'good')\nif good.size == 0:\n    return None\n```\n\niii. `classification` is the verdict of the spike-sorting quality-control classifier described in `ChenLiuEtAl2023_SpikeSortingQC.pdf`.\n\n`units/unit_quality` ('good' / 'multi') is deliberately not used: it is an older label that disagrees on 12.2% of the classifier-good units and is far more permissive.\n\nThe one dropped session (`sub-440958_ses-20190216T162508`) has `classification` and `anno_name` set to NaN for all 1,852 units, i.e. it was never quality-controlled. Excluding it gives 173 sessions and 69,453 good units, against the white paper's 173 sessions and 69,943 units.\n\n## 2-d. How is the per-trial `neural` data aligned to the event described in the `instructions`?\n\ni. Spike times and event times are already on the same session-absolute clock, so no alignment step is needed. The bin edges relative to the go cue are added to each trial's go-cue time to give the absolute time window for that trial, and the spikes are binned against those edges directly.\n\nii.\n```python\ngo = np.asarray(bev['go_start_times'].timestamps)\n```\n\n```python\nedges = (go[:, None] + REL_EDGES[None, :]).ravel()\nrates = np.empty((good.size, n_trials, N_BINS), np.float32)\nfor r, u in enumerate(good):\n    s = allst[starts[u]:offs[u]]\n    pos = np.searchsorted(s, edges).reshape(n_trials, N_BINS + 1)\n    rates[r] = np.diff(pos, axis=1)\n```\n\niii. Everything in the NWB file is timestamped on one global clock, so aligning to the go cue only requires looking up each trial's go-cue time and taking the window around it. There is no resampling or interpolation, and no per-stream offset to correct.\n\n## 2-e. How is the `neural` data temporally binned/resampled?\n\ni. Spike times are binned into 80 non-overlapping 50 ms bins spanning -2.5 s to +1.5 s relative to the go cue. The bin grid is defined once, as 81 edges relative to the go cue, and reused for every trial and session, so every trial has the same 80 timepoints.\n\nii.\n```python\n# trial window relative to the go cue, and bin width, in seconds\nT_START, T_STOP = -2.5, 1.5\nBIN = 0.05\nN_BINS = int(round((T_STOP - T_START) / BIN))             \n\nREL_EDGES = T_START + BIN * np.arange(N_BINS + 1)         \nCENTERS = REL_EDGES[:-1] + BIN / 2                        \n```\n\n```python\nedges = (go[:, None] + REL_EDGES[None, :]).ravel()\n```\n\niii. The window and the 50 ms bin width are set by the instructions. Defining the grid once as offsets from the go cue gives a constant 80 timepoints per trial, which the target format requires.\n\n## 3-a. What variables in the raw data is `input` *time_from_tone_onset* derived from?\n\ni. From `sample_start_times`, the tone onsets of the session, together with the go cue of each trial. The tone taken for a trial is the **last one** before its go cue.\n\nii. The tone of each trial:\n```python\nsample = np.asarray(bev['sample_start_times'].timestamps)\ntone = sample[np.searchsorted(sample, go, side='left') - 1]\n```\n\niii. An early lick replays the sample epoch, so a trial can carry more than one tone; the last one before the go cue is the one the animal actually used.\n\n## 3-b. What processing is involved in computing `input` *time_from_tone_onset*?\n\ni. The bins sit around the go cue, so the value of a bin is its center plus the gap between the tone and the go cue.\n\nii. The bin center, and the shift that turns them into time from the tone:\n```python\nCENTERS = REL_EDGES[:-1] + BIN / 2                        \n```\n```python\n# bins sit around the go cue, values are seconds since the tone\ntime_from_tone = CENTERS[None, :] + (go - tone)[:, None]\n```\n\niii. No additional processing needed other than find the tone onset time.\n\n## 3-c. How is `input` *time_from_tone_onset* aligned with the neural data?\n\ni. It is how the neural binnning grid is defined.\n\nii. The grid, defined once as offsets from the go cue, and laid on each trial's go cue to bin the spikes:\n```python\nT_START, T_STOP = -2.5, 1.5\nBIN = 0.05\nN_BINS = int(round((T_STOP - T_START) / BIN))             \n\nREL_EDGES = T_START + BIN * np.arange(N_BINS + 1)         \nCENTERS = REL_EDGES[:-1] + BIN / 2                        \n```\n```python\nedges = (go[:, None] + REL_EDGES[None, :]).ravel()\n```\n\niii. N/A\n\n## 4-a. What variables in the raw data is `input` *photostim* derived from?\n\ni. From `photostim_onset` and `photostim_duration` in the trials table, with `start_time` and the go cue used to place them on the trial's time axis.\n\nii. The onset and offset of the stimulation, relative to the go cue:\n```python\non_s = trials['photostim_onset'].values\n#!/usr/bin/env python3\n\"\"\"Convert the Brain-wide Activity Map dataset (DANDI 000363) to the decoder format.\n\n    python -u convert_data.py <outpicklefile> [--full | --sample] [--datadir DIR]\n\"\"\"\n\nimport argparse\nimport glob\nimport os\nimport pickle\nimport re\nimport sys\nimport time\n\nimport numpy as np\nfrom pynwb import NWBHDF5IO\n\n_chen2024_seed = 'x5cidj2hy87s'\nnp.random.seed(sum(ord(c) for c in _chen2024_seed) % 2**31)\n\nHERE = os.path.dirname(os.path.abspath(__file__))\n# Default only, for running this by hand from manual/chen2024/. The oracle arm runs\n# the script from /solution while the dataset is mounted read-only at /app/data, so\n# solve.sh overrides this with --datadir.\nDATA_DIR = os.path.join(HERE, 'data')\n\n# trial window relative to the go cue, and bin width, in seconds\nT_START, T_STOP = -2.5, 1.5\nBIN = 0.05\nN_BINS = int(round((T_STOP - T_START) / BIN))             # 80\n\nREL_EDGES = T_START + BIN * np.arange(N_BINS + 1)         # 81 edges, re go cue\nCENTERS = REL_EDGES[:-1] + BIN / 2                        # 80 bin centres\n\nOUTCOME_CODE = {'ignore': 0, 'miss': 1, 'hit': 2}\nEARLY_CODE = {'no early': 0, 'early': 1}\nSIDE_CODE = {'left': 0, 'right': 1}\nCHOICE_NO_LICK = 2               # no lick in the response window\nTONGUE_HIDDEN = 3                # no visible tongue frame in the bin\n\nTONGUE_CONF = 0.5                # tracking likelihood for the tongue to count as visible\nTONGUE_PCT = (40, 60)            # per-session percentiles -> 3 visible classes\n\nINPUT_NAMES = ['time_from_tone_onset', 'photostim']\nOUTPUT_NAMES = ['choice', 'outcome', 'early_lick', 'tongue_y_position']\n\n# output_values[i][code] names each value of output i\nOUTPUT_VALUES = [\n    ['left', 'right', 'no lick'],\n    ['ignore', 'miss', 'hit'],\n    ['no', 'yes'],\n    ['below 40th pct', '40th to 60th pct', 'above 60th pct', 'not visible'],\n]\n\n\ndef region_label(anno):\n    \"\"\"'Orbital area, lateral part, layer 5' -> 'orbital area'.\"\"\"\n    return re.split(r'[,./]', anno)[0].strip().lower()\n\n\ndef _text(col):\n    \"\"\"Read a text column; non-str entries (unlabelled sessions) become ''.\"\"\"\n    return np.array([x if isinstance(x, str) else '' for x in col[:]])\n\n\ndef _bin_mean(idx, y, n):\n    \"\"\"Mean of y per bin given a per-sample bin index. NaN where a bin is empty.\"\"\"\n    ok = ~np.isnan(y)\n    tot = np.bincount(idx[ok], weights=y[ok], minlength=n)\n    cnt = np.bincount(idx[ok], minlength=n)\n    with np.errstate(invalid='ignore'):\n        return np.where(cnt > 0, tot / np.maximum(cnt, 1), np.nan)\n\n\ndef tongue_output(nwb, go):\n    \"\"\"Discretise tongue y into (n_trials, N_BINS) classes.\"\"\"\n    ts = nwb.acquisition['BehavioralTimeSeries'].time_series['Camera0_side_TongueTracking']\n    t_cam = np.asarray(ts.timestamps)\n    data = ts.data[:]                        # (n_frames, 3) = x, y, likelihood\n    y = data[:, 1].copy()\n    y[data[:, 2] < TONGUE_CONF] = np.nan     # keep only visible frames\n\n    # bin the whole session on one grid, then take percentiles of the bin means\n    gidx = np.floor((t_cam - t_cam[0]) / BIN).astype(np.int64)\n    edges = np.nanpercentile(_bin_mean(gidx, y, int(gidx[-1]) + 1), TONGUE_PCT)\n\n    # per trial, bin the same way and digitise against those edges\n    cls = np.full((len(go), N_BINS), TONGUE_HIDDEN, np.int8)\n    lo = np.searchsorted(t_cam, go + T_START, 'left')\n    hi = np.searchsorted(t_cam, go + T_STOP, 'left')\n    for i in range(len(go)):\n        b = np.floor((t_cam[lo[i]:hi[i]] - (go[i] + T_START)) / BIN).astype(np.int64)\n        np.clip(b, 0, N_BINS - 1, out=b)\n        m = _bin_mean(b, y[lo[i]:hi[i]], N_BINS)\n        ok = ~np.isnan(m)\n        cls[i, ok] = np.digitize(m[ok], edges)\n    return cls\n\n\ndef process_session(path):\n    \"\"\"Convert one NWB file. Returns a dict, or None if the session is dropped.\"\"\"\n    with NWBHDF5IO(path, mode='r', load_namespaces=True) as io:\n        nwb = io.read()\n        units = nwb.units\n        trials = nwb.trials.to_dataframe()\n        bev = nwb.acquisition['BehavioralEvents'].time_series\n\n        # ---- units: QC classifier verdict ----------------------------------\n        cls = _text(units['classification'])\n        good = np.flatnonzero(cls == 'good')\n        if good.size == 0:\n            return None\n        regions = [region_label(a) for a in _text(units['anno_name'])[good]]\n\n        # all NWB times are session-absolute seconds\n        go = np.asarray(bev['go_start_times'].timestamps)\n        assert len(go) == len(trials), f'{len(go)} go cues vs {len(trials)} trials'\n\n        # ---- trials filtering ----\n        # spike data\n        # obs_intervals gives one [start, stop] per observed trial, which in some\n        # sessions is fewer than the behavioural trials. \n        # a behavioural trial is observed if its start time is one of the interval starts\n        obs = np.asarray(units['obs_intervals'][good[0]])        \n        keep = np.isin(trials['start_time'].values, obs[:, 0])\n        assert keep.sum() == len(obs), f'{keep.sum()} matched vs {len(obs)} observed'\n\n        # filter no water trials\n        keep &= trials['free_water'].values == 0\n        \n        # a sessioon has to have at least 2 trials according to the instruction\n        if keep.sum() < 2:\n            return None\n        \n        trials = trials[keep]\n        go = go[keep]\n        n_trials = len(go)\n\n        # last tone onset before the go cue; an early lick replays the sample epoch\n        sample = np.asarray(bev['sample_start_times'].timestamps)\n        tone = sample[np.searchsorted(sample, go, side='left') - 1]\n\n        # ---- inputs --------------------------------------------------------\n        # bins sit around the go cue, values are seconds since the tone\n        time_from_tone = CENTERS[None, :] + (go - tone)[:, None]\n\n        # photostim onsets are stored as strings relative to trial start\n        on_s = trials['photostim_onset'].values\n        has = on_s != 'N/A'\n        stim_on = np.full(n_trials, np.nan)\n        stim_on[has] = trials['start_time'].values[has] + on_s[has].astype(float) - go[has]\n        stim_off = np.full(n_trials, np.nan)\n        stim_off[has] = stim_on[has] + trials['photostim_duration'].values[has].astype(float)\n        # NaN compares False, so non-stim trials stay 0\n        photostim = ((CENTERS[None, :] >= stim_on[:, None])\n                     & (CENTERS[None, :] < stim_off[:, None]))\n\n        inp = np.stack([time_from_tone, photostim], axis=1).astype(np.float32)\n\n        # ---- outputs -------------------------------------------------------\n        # choice is not stored; derive it from instruction x outcome\n        outcome_s = trials['outcome'].values\n        side = np.array([SIDE_CODE[x] for x in trials['trial_instruction'].values])\n        choice = np.where(outcome_s == 'ignore', CHOICE_NO_LICK,\n                          np.where(outcome_s == 'hit', side, 1 - side))\n\n        # per-trial values are repeated across bins so all outputs share one array\n        out = np.empty((n_trials, len(OUTPUT_NAMES), N_BINS), np.int8)\n        out[:, 0, :] = choice[:, None]\n        out[:, 1, :] = np.array([OUTCOME_CODE[x] for x in outcome_s])[:, None]\n        out[:, 2, :] = np.array([EARLY_CODE[x] for x in trials['early_lick'].values])[:, None]\n        out[:, 3, :] = tongue_output(nwb, go)\n\n        # ---- neural --------------------------------------------------------\n        # spike_times is ragged: read the buffer once instead of one read per unit\n        offs = np.asarray(units['spike_times'].data)\n        allst = np.asarray(units['spike_times'].target.data)\n        starts = np.concatenate([[0], offs[:-1]])\n\n        edges = (go[:, None] + REL_EDGES[None, :]).ravel()\n        rates = np.empty((good.size, n_trials, N_BINS), np.float32)\n        for r, u in enumerate(good):\n            s = allst[starts[u]:offs[u]]\n            # running spike total at each edge; differencing gives the count per bin\n            pos = np.searchsorted(s, edges).reshape(n_trials, N_BINS + 1)\n            rates[r] = np.diff(pos, axis=1)\n        rates /= BIN                                  # counts -> Hz\n\n        return {\n            'session_id': nwb.identifier,\n            'subject': nwb.subject.subject_id,\n            'neural': [np.ascontiguousarray(rates[:, t, :]) for t in range(n_trials)],\n            'input': [inp[t] for t in range(n_trials)],\n            'output': [out[t] for t in range(n_trials)],\n            'regions': regions,\n            'n_trials': n_trials,\n            'n_units': int(good.size),\n        }\n\n\ndef assemble(results):\n    \"\"\"Stitch per-session results into the target dictionary.\"\"\"\n    subjects = sorted({r['subject'] for r in results})\n    sub_ix = {s: i for i, s in enumerate(subjects)}\n\n    brain_regions = sorted({g for r in results for g in r['regions']})\n    reg_ix = {g: i for i, g in enumerate(brain_regions)}\n\n    return {\n        'neural': [r['neural'] for r in results],\n        'input': [r['input'] for r in results],\n        'output': [r['output'] for r in results],\n\n        'subjects': subjects,\n        'subject_idx': np.array([sub_ix[r['subject']] for r in results], np.int32),\n\n        'brain_regions': brain_regions,\n        'brain_region_idx': [np.array([reg_ix[g] for g in r['regions']], np.int32)\n                             for r in results],\n\n        'input_names': INPUT_NAMES,\n        'output_names': OUTPUT_NAMES,\n        'output_values': OUTPUT_VALUES,\n\n        'metadata': {\n            'task_description':\n                'Auditory delayed-response task. A 3 kHz or 12 kHz tone (0.65 s '\n                'sample epoch) instructs a left or right lick, followed by a 1.2 s '\n                'delay; a 6 kHz go cue opens a 1.5 s response window. Licking '\n                'during sample or delay replays that epoch. tone[:, None]).astype(np.float32)   # (n_trials, NBINS)\n\n        stim_iv = photostim_intervals(f, trial_start, go_all)\n        photostim = np.zeros((len(trial_idx), NBINS), dtype=np.float32)\n        if len(stim_iv):\n            for a, b in stim_iv:\n                # a bin is 'on' if the stimulation overlaps the bin\n                photostim[(edges_abs[:, 1:] > a) & (edges_abs[:, :-1] < b)] = 1.0\n        timing['input'] = time.time() - t0\n\n        # ---------------- outputs -----------------------------------------------------\n        t0 = time.time()\n        oc = outcome[trial_idx]\n# Dataset Conversion Notes\n\n## Overview\n- **Dataset**: Brain-wide neural activity underlying memory-guided movement (Chen et al.), NWB files in /app/data\n- **Date started**: (see file timestamps)\n- **Goal**: Convert to decoder-compatible format\n\n## Step 0: Setup and Initialization\n**Status**: COMPLETE\n\nDirectory contents of /app:\n- `.manifest`, `Dockerfile`, `docker-compose.yaml`\n- `ChenLiuEtAl2023_SpikeSortingQC.pdf` (spike sorting/QC white paper)\n- `datapaper.pdf` (Chen et al., Brain-wide neural activity underlying memory-guided movement)\n- `methodpaper.pdf` (Wang, Kurgyis et al. 2025, Brain-wide analysis reveals movement encoding...)\n- `methods.txt` (methods excerpts)\n- `code/` (MapVideoAnalysis repo: VideoAnalysisUtils/, Sherlock/, Notebooks/, Archive/)\n- `data/` (DANDI 000363 subset: 28 `sub-*` folders, 174 NWB files, `dandiset.yaml`)\n- `decoder.py`, `train_decoder.py` (decoder validation code)\n\nEnvironment verified: python3 with numpy 2.4.4, torch 2.6.0+cu124, h5py 3.16.0.\n\n---\n\n## Step 1: Reference Code Exploration\n**Status**: COMPLETE\n\n### Key Functions Identified\n| Function | File | Stage | Purpose |\n|----------|------|-------|---------|\n| `process_all_sess_parallel(bw, stride, begin_time, end_time, data_folder, save_folder, qc_mode, n_cpu)` | `Sherlock/preprocess_all_ephys.py` -> `VideoAnalysisUtils/preprocessing_DJ_2022Aug.py` | LOADING | Top-level entry. Variable names map 1:1 onto NWB fields (see Step 4).\n- Neural processing: spikes aligned to the **go cue**, binned with a **40 ms sliding window** and converted to **rates in Hz** (divide by bin width). The stride (3.4 ms) equals the video frame period, chosen so that neural bins align with video frames. Our task specifies **50 ms non-overlapping bins**, i.e. bw = stride = 50 ms (documented deviation required by the decoder spec).\n- Neuron curation: **only classifier-'good' units** (region-specific logistic-regression classifiers described in the QC white paper) **that also have a CCF annotation** are used.\n- Trial curation for the *reference analyses*: photostim, free/auto water, early-lick and no-response (ignore) trials are excluded. Our decoder must *predict* early lick and outcome (ignore/miss/hit) and *receives photostimulation as an input*, so those trials must be **kept** (documented deviation).\n- No dF/F is needed (electrophysiology).\n- Additional neuron filter used in the method paper analyses: neurons with mean firing rate **< 2 Hz excluded**; in this conversion this would discard 33% of good units and remove the sparse-firing population that still carries decodable information, so it is **not** applied (documented in Step 5).\n\n---\n\n## Step 2: Dataset Exploration\n**Status**: COMPLETE\n\n### Data Structure\n- `/app/data/dandiset.yaml` + 28 subject folders `sub-<id>/`, 174 NWB (HDF5, NWB 2.6) files named\n  `sub-<id>_ses-<YYYYMMDDTHHMMSS>_behavior+ecephys+ogen.nwb` (DANDI 000363, Chen et al. divided by bin width -> **rate in Hz**, float32 | `sliding_histogram`, `process_one_area` | same rate definition as reference, bin width/stride set to 50 ms by the task spec |\n| `sample_start_times` (last one before the go cue) | `input[0]` = 'time from tone onset (s)' | bin-center time minus tone onset time, seconds, float32 | new (spec) | continuous, time-varying |\n| `photostim_start_times` / `photostim_stop_times` | `input[1]` = 'photostimulation on' | 1 if the bin overlaps a stim interval else 0 | `task_stimulation` in reference | binary, time-varying |\n| `trials/outcome` + `trials/trial_instruction` | `output[0]` = 'lick direction choice' | ignore->'no lick'; hit->instruction; miss->opposite of instruction | `behavior_report`, `task_trial_type` | cross-checked against first lick after the go cue (99.4% agreement) |\n| `trials/outcome` | `output[1]` = 'outcome' | ignore=0, miss=1, hit=2 | `behavior_report` | |\n| `trials/early_lick` | `output[2]` = 'early lick' | 'no early'=0, 'early'=1 | `behavior_early_report` | |\n| `Camera0_side_TongueTracking/data` (y, likelihood) | `output[3]` = 'tongue y-position' | per bin: visible frames = likelihood > 0.9; if none -> 3 ('not visible'); else mean y -> 0/1/2 using the session's 40th/60th percentiles | `align_markers.py` (marker/go-cue alignment) | percentiles computed per session over all visible bins of that session |\n| `units/anno_name` + electrode CCF `x` | `brain_region_idx` | CCF leaf -> coarse group (ALM, Striatum, Thalamus, Midbrain, Medulla, Pons, Cerebellum, Hypothalamus, Hippocampus, Orbital, OtherCortex, Olfactory, CorticalSubplate, Pallidum) x hemisphere (ML >= 5700 um = left) | `helper_get_neuron_id_area` | same 14 groups and same midline as the reference code |\n| `general/subject/subject_id` | `subjects`, `subject_idx` | string id per session | | 28 mice |\n\n### Key Decisions\n1. **Neuron curation = `units/classification == 'good'`**: this column is exactly the output of the region-specific QC classifiers described in the white paper and used by the reference code (`qc_mode='classifier'`). No further firing-rate threshold is applied: the method paper's 2-Hz cut was specific to its ridge-regression encoding analysis, would remove 33% of the units, and the decoder benefits from all recorded units.\n2. **Trial curation**: drop only `auto_water` and `free_water` trials (1,339 + 2,450; reward not driven by the animal's choice, and the reference `get_regular_trial_mask` also drops them). Early-lick, ignore/miss and photostim trials are **kept** because the decoder must predict early lick and outcome and receives photostim as an input; dropping them would make three of the four outputs degenerate.\n3. **No coverage-based trial filtering**: spikes and video exist only inside [trial start, trial stop]. Error (miss) trials are terminated ~0.8 s after the go cue, so requiring the whole [-2.5, +1.5] s window to be observed would delete 95% of miss trials. Instead the window is cut from the **absolute** session time base, so every spike/frame that was recorded in the window (including from the neighbouring trial) is used, and the short inter-trial gaps contribute zero spikes / 'not visible'. Worst-case coverage is 66% of the window, mean ~97%.\n4. **Rates in Hz** (spike count / 0.05 s), as in `sliding_histogram(rate=True)`.\n5. **Choice from the trial table** (outcome x instruction) rather than from lick times: it is the same variable the reference code uses (`behavior_report`), is defined for every trial, and agrees with the first-lick-after-go-cue definition on 99.4% of trials.\n6. **Tongue visibility threshold 0.9** on the DLC likelihood: the likelihood distribution is strongly bimodal (99.8% of frames are <0.1 or >0.9), so the exact threshold is irrelevant.\n7. **Per-session tongue percentiles** computed over the visible bins of that session's extracted windows, exactly as the spec states ('per-session discretization').\n8. **Brain regions are hemisphere-specific** ('left ALM', 'right Medulla', ...), matching the reference code's `left_/right_` area split.\n9. **All 173 sessions with >=1 good unit are kept** (the 174th has no good units). No behavioral-performance session filter is applied: the DANDI release already contains the sessions the authors published, and dropping low-performance sessions would remove error trials needed for the outcome output.\n\n### Planned Sanity Checks\n- [x] Number of good units per coarse region vs data-paper Fig. 1J numbers.\n- [x] 173 sessions / 28 mice / 659 insertions vs paper (173 / 28 / 655-660).\n- [x] Behavioral performance ~84%, trials/session ~476-546.\n- [ ] Independent re-computation of binned rates for a random (session, trial, neuron) directly from the NWB file (`np.allclose`).\n- [ ] Independent re-computation of the photostim input and the time-from-tone input for random trials.\n- [ ] Independent re-computation of the tongue class for random trials, and check the class frequencies are ~40/20/40 among visible bins.\n- [ ] Choice/outcome/early-lick distributions in the converted data match the raw trial-table distributions.\n- [ ] Per-trial neural array shape (n_neurons, 80) and constant n_neurons within a session.\n\n---\n\n## Step 6: Script Development\n**Status**: COMPLETE\n\n`/app/convert_data.py` implements the plan of Step 5:\n\n1. `process_session(path)` opens one NWB file with `h5py` and\n   * selects **good units**: `units/classification == 'good'` and a non-empty `units/anno_name`\n     (reference `qc_mode='classifier'` + histology requirement),\n   * assigns each unit a region `'<hemisphere> <coarse CCF group>'`; hemisphere from the CCF ML\n     coordinate of the unit's electrode with the reference midline `ML = 5700 um`,\n   * selects trials: drops `auto_water`/`free_water` trials (reference `get_regular_trial_mask`),\n     trials outside the units' `obs_intervals`, and trials with no recorded spikes at all,\n   * bins spikes into **80 non-overlapping 50 ms bins** covering [go - 2.5 s, go + 1.5 s] with\n     `np.searchsorted` on the absolute spike times, dividing by the bin width to obtain **Hz**\n     (reference `sliding_histogram(..., rate=True)`),\n   * builds the inputs (time from instruction-tone onset; photostimulation on/off per bin),\n   * builds the outputs (choice, outcome, early lick, discretized tongue y).\n2. `main()` runs the sessions in a `multiprocessing.Pool` (16 workers) and assembles the final dict.\n3. `--show-processing` writes `processing_<session_id>.png` with: raw spike raster vs binned rates for\n   the same trial, population PSTH split by choice, the two inputs, the tongue-y histogram with the\n   40th/60th percentile cuts, the tongue class raster and the per-trial outputs.\n\nCode inefficiencies identified:\n- Reading `units/spike_times` per unit from HDF5 is slow -> the whole ragged array is read once and\n  sliced with the index vector.\n- Binning with nested Python loops (as in the reference `sliding_histogram`) is O(n_bins x n_trials)\n  per unit -> replaced by one `np.searchsorted` per unit over all bin edges (vectorised over trials).\n- Averaging the 3.4 ms video frames inside each 50 ms bin -> done with cumulative sums, no loop.\n\nCode speedups added: single-pass HDF5 reads, `searchsorted` binning, cumsum-based video binning and\n16-way multiprocessing over sessions. Result: **~0.5 s per session**.\n\n### Issues found while developing (and fixed)\n1. **All-zero trials**: in 8 of 173 sessions the ephys recording covers only a contiguous subset of the\n   behavioural trials. The units' `obs_intervals` reveal this; trials outside them are now dropped\n   (`observed_trial_mask`).\n2. **Last trial of a truncated recording**: one further trial can be listed in `obs_intervals` while the\n   probe was already off. Trials whose extracted window contains no spikes at all are dropped.\n3. last 0.5 s of the delay.\n\n| Statistic | Value |\n|---|---|\n| Sessions | 173 |\n| Mice | 28 |\n| Neurons (QC-'good' units) | 69,453 (mean 401 per session, range 90-923) |\n| Trials | 89,544 (mean 518 per session, range 159-796) |\n| Time bins per trial | 80 x 50 ms, from 2.5 s before to 1.5 s after the go cue |\n| Brain regions | 28 (14 coarse CCF groups x hemisphere) |\n| File size | 11.9 GB (`converted_data.pkl`) |\n\n## How to load\n\n```python\nimport pickle\nwith open('/app/converted_data.pkl', 'rb') as f:\n    data = pickle.load(f)\n\nneural = data['neural'][session][trial]   # (n_neurons, 80) float32, firing rate in Hz\ninputs = data['input'][session][trial]    # (2, 80)  float32\noutputs = data['output'][session][trial]  # (4, 80)  int64 category labels\n```\n\n## Format specification\n\n| Key | Contents |\n|---|---|\n| `neural` | list of sessions -> list of trials -> `(n_neurons, 80)` float32 **firing rates in Hz** (spike count per 50 ms bin / 0.05 s) |\n| `input` | `(2, 80)` float32 per trial: `time_from_tone_onset` (s, continuous) and `photostim_on` (0/1) |\n| `output` | `(4, 80)` int64 per trial: `choice`, `outcome`, `early_lick`, `tongue_y_position` |\n| `subjects` / `subject_idx` | 28 mouse ids; index of the mouse for each session |\n| `brain_regions` / `brain_region_idx` | 28 region names (`'left ALM'`, `'right Medulla'`, ...); region index of every neuron |\n| `input_names`, `output_names`, `output_values` | names of the inputs/outputs and of each output category |\n| `metadata` | task description, `time_bin_size` = 50 ms, `temporal_alignment_event` = go cue onset, `off_start` = -2.5, `off_end` = +1.5, curation rules, per-session info |\n\n### Output categories\n| Output | 0 | 1 | 2 | 3 |\n|---|---|---|---|---|\n| `choice` | no lick | left | right | - |\n| `outcome` | ignore | miss | hit | - |\n| `early_lick` | no | yes | - | - |\n| `tongue_y_position` | < 40th pctile | 40-60th pctile | > 60th pctile | not visible |\n\nThe tongue percentiles are computed **per session** over all bins in which the DeepLabCut likelihood\nexceeds 0.9.\n\n## Curation applied\n\n- **Neurons**: only units with `units/classification == 'good'` (the region-specific QC classifiers of\n  Chen, Liu et al. 2023) that also carry a CCF annotation — the same criterion as the reference code.\n- **Trials**: auto-water and free-water trials removed; trials outside the units' `obs_intervals`\n  (i.e. not covered by the ephys recording) and trials without a single recorded spike removed.\n  Early-lick, no-response and photostimulation trials are **kept** because they are decoder targets or\n  inputs.\n- **Sessions**: the one file without any QC-good unit is skipped, leaving the 173 sessions reported in\n  the data paper.\n\n## Reproducing\n\n```bash\npython -u /app/convert_data.py /app/converted_data.pkl --full          # ~45 s with 16 workers\npython -u /app/convert_data.py /app/sample_data.pkl --sample --show-processing\npython -u /app/train_decoder.py /app/converted_data.pkl --plot-samples\n```\n\n## Decoder performance (validation balanced accuracy)\n\n| Output | Accuracy | Chance As in the\n    reference alignment script the marker stream is aligned to the go cue; here\n    all frames falling inside a bin are averaged (the reference used the last\n    frame of each 3.4 ms bin, which for a 3.4 ms bin is the same operation).\n    Frames with DLC likelihood <= threshold are 'tongue not visible'.\n    \"\"\"\n    bt = f['acquisition/BehavioralTimeSeries']\n    key = None\n    for k in ('Camera0_side_TongueTracking', 'Camera3_side_TongueTracking'):\n        if k in bt:\n            key = k\n            break\n    ntrials = edges_abs.shape[0]\n    if key is None:\n        return (np.full((ntrials, NBINS), np.nan), np.zeros((ntrials, NBINS), dtype=bool))\n\n    data = bt[key]['data'][:]\n    ts = bt[key]['timestamps'][:]\n    y = data[:, 1]\n    lik = data[:, 2]\n    visible = (lik > TONGUE_LIKELIHOOD_THRESHOLD) & np.isfinite(y)\n\n    # cumulative sums let us average the frames inside every bin without a loop\n    yv = np.where(visible, y, 0.0)\n    cs_y = np.concatenate([[0.0], np.cumsum(yv)])\n    cs_n = np.concatenate([[0], np.cumsum(visible.astype(np.int64))])\n    idx = np.searchsorted(ts, edges_abs)                  # (ntrials, NBINS+1)\n    lo, hi = idx[:, :-1], idx[:, 1:]\n    nvis = cs_n[hi] - cs_n[lo]\n    sumy = cs_y[hi] - cs_y[lo]\n    with np.errstate(invalid='ignore', divide='ignore'):\n        mean_y = np.where(nvis > 0, sumy / np.maximum(nvis, 1), np.nan)\n    return mean_y, nvis > 0\n\n\ndef discretize_tongue(mean_y, visible):\n    \"\"\"0: < 40th pctile, 1: 40-60th pctile, 2: > 60th pctile, 3: not visible.\n\n    Percentiles are computed per session over all bins in which the tongue is visible.\n    \"\"\"\n    cls = np.full(mean_y.shape, 3, dtype=np.int64)\n    vals = mean_y[visible]\n    if vals.size == 0:\n        return cls\n    p40, p60 = np.percentile(vals, [40, 60])\n    cls[visible & (mean_y < p40)] = 0\n    cls[visible & (mean_y >= p40) & (mean_y <= p60)] = 1\n    cls[visible & (mean_y > p60)] = 2\n    return cls\n\n\n# ------------------------------------------------------------------------- plotting\ndef plot_processing(res, path, go, tone, edges_abs, tongue_y, tongue_visible, plot_dir):\n    \"\"\"Visualise every processing step for one session.\"\"\"\n    import matplotlib\n    matplotlib.use('Agg')\n    import matplotlib.pyplot as plt\n\n    sess = res['session_id']\n    neural = res['neural']\n    inputs = res['input']\n    outputs = res['output']\n    ntrials = len(neural)\n    tt = BIN_CENTERS\n\n    fig, ax = plt.subplots(4, 2, figsize=(15, 14))\n\n    # No further firing-rate threshold is applied: the method paper's 2-Hz cut was specific to its ridge-regression encoding analysis, would remove 33% of the units, and the decoder benefits from all recorded units.\n2. **Trial curation**: drop only `auto_water` and `free_water` trials (1,339 + 2,450; reward not driven by the animal's choice, and the reference `get_regular_trial_mask` also drops them). Early-lick, ignore/miss and photostim trials are **kept** because the decoder must predict early lick and outcome and receives photostim as an input; dropping them would make three of the four outputs degenerate.\n3. **No coverage-based trial filtering**: spikes and video exist only inside [trial start, trial stop]. Error (miss) trials are terminated ~0.8 s after the go cue, so requiring the whole [-2.5, +1.5] s window to be observed would delete 95% of miss trials. Instead the window is cut from the **absolute** session time base, so every spike/frame that was recorded in the window (including from the neighbouring trial) is used, and the short inter-trial gaps contribute zero spikes / 'not visible'.
